title: Lessons 4 6
description: Multiple-choice question bank. Each question has four options and one correct answer.

questions.question: A student wants to compare the number of students who selected different favorite colors. Which chart is the most suitable?

options.text: Bar chart
Line chart
Pie chart showing a timeline
Flowchart

questions.question: Why is it important to add headings to charts and graphs?

options.text: To make the chart harder to read
To use more space
To explain what the chart shows and help readers understand the data
To hide the data values

questions.question: After creating three different charts, your teacher asks you to choose the best one. What is the best way to decide?

options.text: Choose the chart with the most colours
Choose the first chart you created
Choose the chart with the largest title
Choose the chart that communicates the data most clearly for your purpose

questions.question: Why should similar data be presented using consistent formatting?

options.text: It makes every chart look different
It helps readers compare information and understand it more easily
It removes the need for labels
It changes the values in the data

questions.question: Ben notices that some labels on his chart are cut off and cannot be read clearly. What should he do?

options.text: Adjust the chart size or label settings so the labels are visible
Delete the labels
Make the labels smaller until they disappear
Remove the chart title and all values

questions.question: You notice that your spreadsheet uses different fonts and colors for similar headings. What would you most likely do?

options.text: Add even more fonts and colours
Remove all headings
Apply consistent formatting to similar headings
Change the data values

questions.question: Before submitting your spreadsheet, you remember to save your work. What does this show?

options.text: You are changing the original data
You are making the spreadsheet public
You are deleting earlier work
You are taking steps to keep your work and avoid losing changes

questions.question: When making a chart from a table, what data must you select?

options.text: Only the spreadsheet title
The relevant data values and their category or time labels, including headings where appropriate
Every empty cell in the worksheet
Only the cells containing formulas unrelated to the chart

questions.question: Which of the following is a reason for reflecting on digital work?

options.text: To avoid learning anything new
To identify what went well and what could be improved
To delete the finished project
To make the task take longer

questions.question: Reflecting on a completed activity allows a person to:

options.text: Forget every step they completed
Avoid listening to others
Identify strengths, difficulties, and lessons learned
Change the past results

questions.question: What should conclude the reflection process?

options.text: Set useful targets or actions for future improvement
Ignore the problems that were found
Delete the project
Repeat the same mistakes

questions.question: Which is a true benefit of reflecting on one's own work?

options.text: It guarantees that no mistakes will ever happen
It removes the need to practise
It makes feedback unnecessary
It helps a person improve future work by learning from experience

questions.question: Evaluating the process and outcome of an activity is best defined as:

options.text: Copying someone else's work
Reflection
Data entry
Formatting

questions.question: A student regrets choosing “Colours” over “Foods,” citing less varied responses. What are they evaluating?

options.text: The computer's storage space
The presentation font
The choice of investigation topic and its suitability
The classroom seating plan

questions.question: A student notes neither they nor their partner mastered certain formulas, despite finishing successfully. This reflects:

options.text: An area of weakness or a skill they need to develop
A reason to stop using spreadsheets
Proof that the project was unsuccessful
A need to delete their work

questions.question: Students share reflections and targets aloud, with some noted on the board. This mainly supports:

options.text: Keeping all learning private
Avoiding future targets
Making the project more complicated
Sharing ideas and learning from one another

questions.question: A student notices their partner excelled at slides while they focused on data. This awareness should shape:

options.text: A decision to avoid teamwork
How they divide roles and use each other's strengths in future projects
A decision to remove the slides
The deletion of the data

questions.question: Reflection shows both teammates lacked a needed skill. The most productive response is to:

options.text: Blame one another
Ignore the skill gap
Plan to practise or learn that skill before the next project
Avoid similar projects forever

questions.question: What is the first step in presenting properly?

options.text: Start speaking without preparation
Prepare and organize what you want to say
Read every word as quickly as possible
Choose decorations before understanding the topic

questions.question: What should a presenter do regarding timing and feedback?

options.text: Ignore the time limit and all comments
Finish as quickly as possible without explanation
Speak for as long as they want
Practise to keep within the time limit and listen respectfully to feedback

questions.question: Besides presenting well, what else matters equally?

options.text: Preparing the work and contributing to the team
Using the most expensive computer
Making the presentation as long as possible
Avoiding all questions

questions.question: While presenting, what should a speaker remember to do?

options.text: Face the screen the entire time and speak quietly
Read too quickly to finish early
Speak clearly, face the audience, and explain the main points
Avoid looking at the audience

questions.question: After each team presents, what should classmates give?

options.text: Unrelated stories
Helpful and respectful feedback
Only marks without comments
Personal criticism

questions.question: Which best supports an engaging presentation?

options.text: Reading every slide word for word
Using tiny text and crowded slides
Speaking with your back to the audience
Using clear visuals, simple points, and an understandable speaking style

questions.question: Feedback includes criticism. What is the best response?

options.text: Listen calmly, consider the suggestion, and use helpful advice to improve
Argue with everyone who gives feedback
Ignore all comments immediately
Stop presenting

questions.question: A student values only presenting but not preparation tasks. What mindset shift helps?

options.text: Believe that only the speaker contributes
Avoid sharing responsibilities
Recognize that planning, research, teamwork, and preparation are also important
Let one person do all the work
